name: Pulley
tagline: Cap table and equity management for startups: grants, vesting, SAFEs, option pools, and round modeling.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The math inside a cap table is not hard: shares, classes, vesting schedules, SAFE conversions, a dilution waterfall. An agent can model all of that in a weekend and it will probably agree with Pulley to the share. What you cannot build is the part that matters, which is a record other people accept: your lawyers, your auditors, your acquirer's diligence team, and the employees who need a portal that is not a spreadsheet you emailed them. Equity admin also drags in 409A valuations, board consents, e-signature, 83(b) and Rule 701 tracking, and tax reporting, none of which is a coding problem. Build the model to sanity-check your own dilution, keep paying someone else to be the system of record.
coreLoopDIY: A local cap table model that tracks stakeholders, share classes, grants and vesting, then computes fully diluted ownership and models SAFE conversion and dilution through a priced round.
requirements: Willingness to hand-enter every grant and side letter
A real lawyer for anything you intend to rely on
whatYouLose: 409A valuations and the defensibility that comes with a third party issuing them
Documents your counsel and an acquirer's diligence team will actually accept
E-signature, board consents, and grant acceptance workflows
Employee and investor portals, exercise flows, and option-expiry notices
Tax and compliance tracking: 83(b) reminders, Rule 701 limits, ISO 100k, year-end reporting
moatNotes: Nobody wires an acquisition against a cap table that lives in one founder's SQLite file.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the product being sold is not arithmetic, it is a shared source of truth that lawyers, auditors, employees and investors all agree to look at. A cap table only has value when other parties trust it, and trust here is bought with audit trails, countersigned documents, a 409A opinion with a name on it, and a vendor that will still exist at exit. Add that migrating off mid-fundraise is the worst possible time to discover your model was wrong, and the switching cost does the rest.
notes: The spreadsheet underneath is a weekend; the thing people are buying is not the spreadsheet. The moat is that everyone else in the room, counsel, auditors, acquirers, has agreed to treat this vendor's record as the truth.
prompt:
Build a local-only cap table modeling tool. Stack: TypeScript, Next.js App Router, SQLite via better-sqlite3, Tailwind. No auth, no cloud, no telemetry, no accounts. Single user, runs on localhost.

Data model (migrations in plain SQL, seed script included):
- stakeholders: name, type (founder, employee, investor, entity), email optional
- share_classes: name, type (common, preferred), original issue price, liquidation preference multiple, participating flag, conversion ratio
- issuances: stakeholder, share class, share count, price per share, issue date
- option_pool: authorized shares, plus a reserved/unissued computation
- grants: stakeholder, share count, strike price, grant date, vesting start, cliff months, total months, schedule type (monthly, quarterly), early exercise flag, cancelled_on nullable
- safes: stakeholder, principal, valuation cap, discount, pre or post money flag, MFN flag, date
- convertible_notes: principal, interest rate, cap, discount, maturity

Features, in scope:
1. CRUD screens for every table above. Keyboard friendly, dense tables, no modals where a row edit will do.
2. Vesting engine: given a grant and an as-of date, return vested/unvested shares. Handle cliff, monthly and quarterly accrual, and cancellation.
3. Cap table view: outstanding vs fully diluted ownership per stakeholder, with the unissued option pool shown as its own line, as of any date.
4. Round modeling: enter new money, pre-money valuation, and target post-round pool percentage. Convert all SAFEs and notes correctly (cap vs discount, whichever is better for the holder; pre-money SAFEs dilute each other, post-money SAFEs do not), compute the pool shuffle, and output a before/after ownership table plus a per-stakeholder dilution delta.
5. Exit waterfall: given an exit price, distribute proceeds respecting liquidation preferences, participation, and conversion-to-common where that pays more.
6. CSV import and export for stakeholders, issuances and grants.
7. An /audit page that lists every assumption the model made in the last round calculation, in plain English.

Explicitly out of scope, do not build or fake: 409A valuations, document generation, e-signature, board consents, employee portals, exercise requests, tax forms, Rule 701 or ISO 100k tracking, anything that implies legal reliance.

Write unit tests for the vesting engine, SAFE conversion, and waterfall, including a post-money SAFE case and a participating-preferred-with-cap case. Put a banner on every page: this is a model, not a record, confirm with counsel. Secrets, if any ever appear, go in .env. README explains how to run it and lists the known simplifications.
